content.title: Good work, but incomplete experiments
content.review:
### Main idea
This work points out an potential cause of the adversarial samples: the discontinuity of gradients for Relu activation. It further investigate a more smooth substitute, the soft-plus function, and show incredible improvements on ImageNet dataset.

### Clarity
The writing of this paper is clear and straightforward

### Originality
The argument that the Relu function worsen adversarial robustness has been suggested in some past works. Yet, according to my knowledge, this work is the first one to seriously investigate this problem and propose a solution. Also ,I notice that there is a similar work, who also proposes a new activation for robustness, termed as [Sparta](https://openreview.net/forum?id=iF81jBISQDV) in the submission of ICLR 2021.

### Quality and significance

#### Pros
1. The motivation of this work aligns with the common sense in the domain of adversarial robustness. I myself also believe that, to fully solve the issue of adversarial samples, we need new designs and insights about the architecture of DNN. The proposal of using soft-plus function seems straightforward and reasonable. 
2. The experimental results on ImageNet is really awesome and convincing. The setting of empirical evaluations is also clear and suitable.

#### Cons 
1. This work is short for the most important empirical evaluation setting: defense against PGD20 on CIFAR10, as most of the leading works all present their results of this setting as their main entry. The author claimed the complexity of training ImageNet forces them to adopt FGSM in the adversarial training procedure, yet this problem does not exist in CIFAR10. In fact, I've read [a recent work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.03593) that points out that the soft-plus function may not work on CIFAR10.
2. As stated in the paper, the author believe the soft-plus function can smoothen the gradients and therefore lead to better results. I've seen the improved results in the paper, but I haven't seen any empirical analysis about the gradients of models with or without soft-plus.
3. The content in Section 5 seems somewhat redundant and irrelevant to the main idea. It simply uses the framework of EfficientNet and does not offer any special understandings for adversarial learning. It is more suitable to be presented in the appendix.

### What I expect the author to respond:
1. Verify the effectiveness of your work on CIFAR10 like TRADES and MART.
2. I have a question: Why only using soft-plus in the back-propagation? Is this the key design? Can you explain its motivation or has anyone else tested this scheme before? Can you provide results when using soft-plus in both forward and backward? 
3. Please provide visualization or other statistics that can prove that your method did smoothen gradients. Maybe replace Section 5 with this analysis.

As long as the author can answer these three questions, I will raise my score to 7 or 8.

display_title: Interesting finding, but needs further analysis

content.title: Interesting finding, but needs further analysis
content.review:
############################## Summary ##################################

The paper proposes the use of smooth activation functions for better gradient propagation during attack generation and adversarial training. The authors demonstrate improvement in both adversarial robustness and clean accuracy by replacing ReLU activations with smooth functions during PGD-1 adversarial training on ImageNet dataset, for an $\ell_\infty$ constraint of 4/255. 

############################### Pros #####################################

-  Interesting observation, can potentially give an additional boost in performance
-  Adversarial robustness and clean accuracy improve at no additional computational cost
-  Easy to integrate with any network architecture
-  Scales well to networks of larger depth, width and larger image resolutions
-  Achieves improvement over LLR-2 for ImageNet dataset

############################### Cons #####################################

  -  The paper considers a PGD-1 step (or R-FGSM) defense as baseline. The original PGD-1 step defense with ReLU activation itself might be suffering from gradient masking. In this case, even the proposed defense could also be a result of gradient masking, although the smooth activation function helps with better gradient computation. Absence of gradient masking in single-step defenses needs to be justified using thorough validation as discussed by Carlini et al. [1] using gradient-free attacks such as Square attack and SPSA, black-box transfer based attacks, attacks with multiple steps and multiple random restarts. Also, the sanity checks proposed by Athalye et al. [2] need to be demonstrated. 
  -  Evaluation on PGD-200 step attack is not sufficient. It might happen that there is a large benefit while evaluating against this attack, but only a marginal benefit with stronger attacks such as MultiTargeted attack [3] and AutoAttack [4]. 
  -  Since the paper is an empirical finding, it would require more experimental justification, to validate that it actually works across other datasets and conditions as well. ImageNet has many closely related classes and findings on ImageNet may not generalize well to other datasets. For example, LLR-2 [5] achieves very good results on ImageNet (better than TRADES), however the robust accuracy with their 2-step defense on CIFAR-10 is significantly lesser than TRADES. 
  -  For $\ell_\infty$ robustness, the most widely used benchmark is a threat model of 8/255 on CIFAR-10 dataset. Evaluation on this dataset would enable the reader to get a sense of where the proposed defense stands with respect to all other existing defenses. 
  -  The paper does not mention the impact of using smooth activation functions on multi-step defenses like TRADES.
  -  The key novelty of the paper is the use of smooth activation functions for robustness. However this is also seen in prior works [5].

[1] Carlini et al., On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness, https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.06705

[2] Athalye et al., Obfuscated Gradients Give a False Sense of Security: Circumventing Defenses to Adversarial Examples, ICML 2018

[3] Gowal et al., An Alternative Surrogate Loss for PGD-based Adversarial Testing, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1910.09338.pdf

[4] Croce et al., Reliable Evaluation of Adversarial Robustness with an Ensemble of Diverse Parameter-free Attacks, ICML 2020

[5] Qin et al., Adversarial Robustness through Local Linearization, NeurIPS 2019

########################## Reasons for score #################################

Although the observation is very interesting, and can potentially be useful for adversarial training, the paper needs more thorough evaluation. For example, demonstration that it works on other datasets, better evaluation of the defense and impact on multi-step training. Also the use of smooth activation functions for robustness is seen in prior work. Hence, I vote for rejecting the paper. 

##################### Questions during rebuttal period ###########################

  -  Please address and clarify the cons above 
  -  Could the authors also report the results across multiple reruns, since R-FGSM training is known to be very sensitive to initialization.
  -  While R-FGSM training can give good results for small values of $\varepsilon$, it may not work well with larger $\varepsilon$ values [6]. It would be useful to know whether the proposed solution works well for larger $\varepsilon$ values such as 8/255 
  -  Could the authors share details of the base PGD-1 (or R-FGSM) training (optimizer, learning rate schedule, number of epochs, initial random noise added for R-FGSM attack, training loss, validation split, use of early stopping)? The baseline results seem to be much better than the results reported in FBF [7].

[6] Andriushchenko et al., Understanding and Improving Fast Adversarial Training, NeurIPS 2020

[7] Wong et al. Fast is Better than Free: Revisiting Adversarial Training, ICLR 2020
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

display_title: Impressive empirical results, but has some weaknesses

content.title: Impressive empirical results, but has some weaknesses
content.review:
The paper improves the state-of-the-art of adversarial training on ImageNet by using smooth activation functions and optimizing architectures via neural architecture search. Compared to prior art (Qin et al. [1]), the paper reports clean and adversarial accuracy of 82.2% (+9.5) and 58.6% (+11.6), respectively.

If those results withstand scrutiny, they are pretty impressive and would in my opinion deserve publication in ICLR. The paper also reports on a number of insightful supporting experiments, e.g. exploring different types of smooth activation functions, studying the effect of scaling up the architectures etc., which are systematically designed and carefully described.

However, the paper has several weaknesses:
- It does not follow established protocols for evaluating adversarial robustness as put forward, e.g. in [2]. The authors state that 200 PGD iterations were sufficient for attack convergence - it would be good to corroborate this e.g. by showing plots of attack success rates over the number of PGD iterations. Did the authors use random restarts in PGD (same as Qin et al.)? Plotting the loss landscape around test samples (same as in Qin et al.) and reporting adversarial accuracy for PGD with larger epsilon would be other valuable sanity checks. I don’t want to create unnecessary work for the authors, but there are just too many examples of supposedly great advances in defending against adversarial examples which did not withstand scrutiny (e.g. consider [3]). Related to this: are you planning to release your trained models?
- The paper talks extensively about “better gradients” being the reason for the improved performance of adversarial training, however, it doesn’t give a proper definition of what “good” and “bad” really means, except - inherently - that “good” gradients yield better results. This makes the notion of “better gradients” a rather tautological explanation. Moreover, Figure 1 does not provide sufficient evidence to substantiate the authors’ very general claim that, because “ReLU’s gradient takes an abrupt change, when its input is 0” it “significantly degrades the gradient quality”. Moreover, I find it misleading to denote the columns in Table 1 as
“Improving Gradient Quality”. A priori, this table reports the effects of using smooth activation functions; the conclusion that this may yield improved gradient quality can only be drawn a posteriori. 
- Finally, the paper lacks discussion of related work and prior art, such as the usage of smooth activations in other contexts, but most importantly the relation to Qin et al. [1] who actually seem to be the first ones using smooth activations in adversarial training. Comparing the results with Qin et al., one could arrive actually at the impression that performance gains mostly stem from the neural architecture search rather than from the smooth activations. This needs to be clarified, and proper emphasis should be put on the relative merits of smooth activations vs neural architecture search throughout the paper.

Two minor comments on the “no-free-lunch” in Adversarial Training:
- It is not just “generally believed” that there is a fundamental trade-off between accuracy and robustness; Tsipras et al. (2019) (and others) actually proved that such trade-offs exist.
- There may be a misunderstanding of what this trade-off entails; the final model trained by the authors still incurs degraded clean accuracy compared to a conventionally trained model, which actually confirms the “no-free-lunch” trade-off.

[1] Qin et al., Adversarial robustness through local linearization. In NeurIPS, 2019
[2] N. Carlini et al. https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.06705
[3] L. Engstrom et al. https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.10272

display_title: Interesting idea and results, but too preliminary yet.

content.title: Interesting idea and results, but too preliminary yet.
content.review:
# Smooth adversarial training

### Summary

The paper studies the effect of replacing the ReLU activation by a smoother
approximation on the accuracy and adversarial robustness of SOTA neural network
architectures (ResNet-50 and EfficientNet) on the ImageNet dataset. The authors find
that all the different smooth approximations tested improve _both_ accuracy and
robustness, when applied to the backward path only, and even more when
applied to both the forward and backward path. They confirm previous empirical
results according to which increasing width, depth and input resolution boosts
accuracy and robustness, whatever the activation function. Combining all these
techniques, they claim to beat the state-of-the-art on ImageNet by a high
margin, both in terms of accuracy and of adversarial robustness.


### Overall evaluation

The results are interesting and promising, but still in a preliminary state.

1. _Standard deviations missing_: All the paper is about relative improvements
  over the standard ResNet-50 architecture but does not report a single
  standard deviation. That makes it difficult to evaluate the significance of
  the improvements.
2. _Only one dataset_: The results are tested on ImageNet only: what about other
  standard datasets, such as MNIST, CIFAR10/100, SVHN, CelebA? Since the paper
  is all about empirical results with almost no theory, several datasets +
  standard deviations would seem a least.
3. _Only one attack_: Everything is tested for one single attack type (PGD),
  attack norm ($\ell_\infty$) and attack size ($\epsilon = 4 / 255$). I would
  at least expect that the findings be confirmed with other attack types (in
  particular attacks that do not explicitly use the network's backward path,
  such as the boundary or HopSkipJump attack), attack norms, and for different
  attack sizes (e.g. plot robust acc vs attack-size). I also miss an analysis
  of the influence of the attack/regularization size $\epsilon_{train}$ used
  during adversarial training: your proposed architecture could be more
  efficient for some values of $\epsilon_{train}$ than for others.
4. _Readability & Tables_: Overall, I find the paper difficult to follow. I
  recommend putting **all results in one or two big tables** (not just small
  parts). That's what tables are made for: a concise presentation of many
  results to simplify comparisons.  The text itself could be more concise.
  (Also, current column names of Table 1 are misleading. I suggest making them
  shorter and explain them in the caption. More generally, I would advice
  making tables and figures self-contained: it should be fully understandable
  from reading the caption with as little as possible reference to the main
  text, and if it can't be avoided, then use clear references. Figures are
  there to simplify the reader's work, not harden it by letting him search all
  the info in the text.)

For these reasons, I _currently_ clearly suggest to reject the paper.


### Additional comments/questions

5. _Dependence on network architecture_: Results were only tested on
  architectures with residual connections. What about more classical,
  feed-forward architectures (without skips)? I am especially curious, since
  the fact that input dimension helps robustness contradicts
  [(1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.01421) where it is shown that adversarial
  vulnerability increases with the input dimension.  However, their results
  only hold at initialization (with He init) and for classical feed-forward
  nets without skips. So I'd be curious to know whether the difference comes
  from the architecture, or a better training.
6. _Initialization_: On the same note, how do you initialize? He initialization?
  In particular, He initialization uses a factor 2 to account to for the ReLU
  activation. Do you adjust this factor to account for the different activation
  functions (as in pytorch's `torch.nn.init.calculate_gain(nonlinearity)`)?
7. How do you modify the architecture in higher dimensions? (It can't be exactly
  the same architecture.)
8. Sec 4.2: I disagree with the last part of the last sentence "... rules out
  the effect from having responses when $x < 0$". It might suggest it, but it
  does not rule it out.

(1) First-order adversarial vulnerability of neural networks and input
dimension, ICML 2019, [link](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.01421).
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

display_title: Understanding this paper from the feature transformation flow perspective

content.title: Understanding this paper from the feature transformation flow perspective
content.comment:
Dear Authors,

It is enjoyable to read your paper.  I try to understand the robustness gain by the smoothed ReLu. 

The paper shows that smoothed ReLu can improve adversarial training. 
I am just wondering about the reasons for this benefit gain. 
Can we understand it from the flow perspective? With smoothed ReLu, will the forward propagation of the feature transformation flow become more stable?

replying_to: Replying to Understanding this paper from the feature transformation flow perspective
display_title: Re: Understanding this paper from the feature transformation flow perspective

content.title: Re: Understanding this paper from the feature transformation flow perspective
content.comment:
Thanks for your interest in our work.

Our analysis suggests the main reason for the improvement of smoothed ReLUs is that they have much better gradients in training. As we show in this paper, as long as the networks’ backward pass get smoothed, you can always see performance improvement in adversarial robustness, even if the networks’ forward pass still uses ReLU. 

The idea of explaining the benefits of our methods from the flow perspective sounds interesting. But as I am not an expert in this direction, I am afraid that I may not be able to provide many insightful suggestions. Please feel free to use our codes/models to validate this interesting idea! And let us know if you have any interesting findings or encounter any difficulties in using our codebase.

display_title: A general response to all reviewers

content.title: A general response to all reviewers
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for their valuable comments, which help us to improve the quality of this paper. We see there are several concerns shared by all reviewers (mainly caused by misunderstanding), therefore provide a general response as the following:


---	
**CONCERN 1: only ImageNet results, no results on another dataset like CIFAR-10 & MNIST**

Though we understand that having results on other datasets like CIFAR-10 and MNIST will further enhance our paper, we do not think missing such experiments is a significant concern of our paper (or even should be grounds to rejection). 

CIFAR-10 & MNIST are toy datasets and are generally believed to be much less challenging than ImageNet. The main motivation for still studying these small datasets is that 
1) performing experiments on CIFAR-10 and MNIST are computationally cheap and easy to analyze; 
2) the evaluation on these small datasets usually serves as warm-ups (or sanity checks) for further validating the potential of the proposed method on more challenging datasets like ImageNet. 

However, in our paper, these motivations are no longer valid: 
1) our experiments on ImageNet are already computationally cheap (the training time is 1.5x than standard training); 
2) compared to ImageNet, small datasets like CIFAR-10 and MINST show many issues in the context of adversarial training (e.g., significant overfitting [1,2,3]), which does not necessarily make them easier to analyze (or maybe even resulting in more confusions). 
3) we already show that our method can work pretty well under the large-scale ImageNet dataset. We believe the next important goal is to show generalization on even more challenging datasets, rather than worrying whether our method can work well on MNIST & CIFAR-10.

**Given the arguments above, we strongly argue that experiments on small datasets like CIFAR-10 & MINST are not necessary for our evaluation, and should not be counted as a major concern for rejecting our paper.**



---	
**CONCERN 2: Novelty concern regarding the prior work Qin et al. [4]**

We do not believe our novelty is impaired by the prior work [4] (where softplus activation is used). The message delivered in [4] is kind of mixed---in their Table 2, the authors show that a different training schedule + softplus can improve the ReLU baseline, and attribute this improvement mainly to the utilization of different training schedule, i.e., [4] states “This is largely due to the learning rate schedule used, which is similar to the one used by TRADES”. No other ablations about softplus are provided.

While the message delivered in our SAT paper is much more clear and general:
1) Rather than limiting our target specifically as softplus, we discover the FAMILY of smooth activation functions which all help adversarial training. Besides, compared to the softplus baseline, we find that the best activation function, SILU, can further improve the robustness by more than 2% using ResNet. 
2) Our paper provides a clear explanation on how smooth activation function can help---the key is to make activation functions have continuous gradients (e.g., as shown in Section 3, substitute ReLU’s gradient with a continuous one can also help) 
3) Compared to [4], we provide a more extensive evaluation of utilizing smooth activation functions on a wide range of different network architectures.

Given these results, we disagree with R1 that our paper has novelty concerns. Instead, we agree with R2 that this is a minor concern, and more clarification will address it.



---	
**CONCERN 3: PGD-1 (or R-FGSM) attack for training may lead to gradient masking? Multiple-step adversarial training?**

We want to clarify that PGD-1 and R-FGSM are different---they use different $\epsilon$ for initialization and for the attack step size. Though R-FGSM is shown to have a gradient masking issue, PGD-1 can lead to successful adversarial training, as shown in [5].

To further alleviate the reviewer’s concern, we also perform PGD-5 training and found that SAT still substantially outperforms the ReLU baseline (by more than 5%).



---	
**CONCERN 4: Results on other $\epsilon$?**

We follow the setup in [6] to training networks with $\epsilon$=16 & PGD-30 targeted attacks. We observe consistent improvements---compared to the ReLU baseline, SAT boosts robustness by 6%-7%.

replying_to: Replying to A general response to all reviewers
display_title: A general response to all reviewers (continue)

content.title: A general response to all reviewers (continue)
content.comment:
---	
**CONCERN 5: Results on defending against gradient-free attack?**

We want to reiterate that there is no direct evidence that our method (either the PGD-1 training strategy or the architectural design) causes gradient masking issues. Instead, our SAT even further improves the gradient quality of ReLU, making the whole network differentiable everywhere. For attacking models with gradient issues, gradient-free attacks generally cannot outperform the white-box PGD attacks, and are much more computationally expensive. Therefore, we do not include them in our paper.



---	
**Finally,  to demonstrate that our method is solid and can indeed withstand different evaluation criteria, we released the models here: [anonymized code](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/45c88614-f6b7-4798-8576-d0ed1a092f19/). We welcome all reviewers and public audiences to validate the effectiveness of our method.**


---	
- [1] Uesato, Jonathan, et al. "Are labels required for improving adversarial robustness?." arXiv preprint arXiv:1905.13725 (2019).
- [2] Zhai, Runtian, et al. "Adversarially robust generalization just requires more unlabeled data." arXiv preprint arXiv:1906.00555 (2019).
- [3] Carmon, Yair, et al. "Unlabeled data improves adversarial robustness." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems. 2019.
- [4] Qin, Chongli, et al. "Adversarial robustness through local linearization." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems. 2019.
- [5] Wong, Eric, Leslie Rice, and J. Zico Kolter. "Fast is better than free: Revisiting adversarial training." arXiv preprint arXiv:2001.03994 (2020).
- [6] Xie, Cihang, et al. "Feature denoising for improving adversarial robustness." Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2019.

display_title: Main issue --missing standard deviations-- not addressed; concerns 1&4&5 poorly addressed

content.title: Main issue --missing standard deviations-- not addressed; concerns 1&4&5 poorly addressed
content.comment:
My main issue --the missing standard deviations for all measures-- has not been addressed/mentioned so far.

#### Concern 1 (missing datasets):

Including other datasets, such as CIFAR-10 and MNIST, is not just for "warm-up", but also to check the robustness of the results across multiple datasets. You could include any other datasets as well, if you think that they are more appropriate. But one good reason to do it on CIFAR-10/100, MNIST, SVHN, or any other standard/well-known dataset is that it eases the comparison with others. 
**Anyway, it shouldn't be so difficult to add these experiments, if they are just "warm-up" toy examples...**

#### Reproducibility

> Finally, to demonstrate that our method is solid and can indeed withstand different evaluation criteria, we released the models here: anonymized code. We welcome all reviewers and public audiences to validate the effectiveness of our method."

This is really not an argument: it's the authors' job to do the initial **in depth** evaluation of their method, not the community's.

#### "CONCERN 4: Results on other $\epsilon$? 

> We follow the setup in [6] to training networks with =16 & PGD-30 targeted attacks. We observe consistent improvements compared to the ReLU baseline, SAT boosts robustness by 9%-10%."

Sure, but it's still interesting --and absolutely standard!-- to show results for other attack-sizes $\epsilon_{attack}$ (and maybe also other defence sizes $\epsilon_{train}$.

#### Concern 5

> We want to reiterate that there is no direct evidence that our method (either the PGD-1 training strategy or the architectural design) causes gradient masking issues.

The reason I asked to include black-box attacks in the tests is not to alleviate gradient masking issues. It's because they can be quite different in essence/spirit from PGD and can therefore yield different results. What counts, of course, isn't whether the black-box attack performs better or worse than the PGD attack, but how the different models compare on a same black-box attack.

replying_to: Replying to Main issue --missing standard deviations-- not addressed; concerns 1&4&5 poorly addressed

content.title: Concerns on robustness evaluations
content.comment:
I agree with AnonReviewer4 that, while it is great that you released your trained models, it is the authors' responsibility to carry out a comprehensive robustness evaluation following established recommendations [1] similar as previous works [2].

[1] N. Carlini et al. https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.06705
[2] Qin et al., Adversarial robustness through local linearization. In NeurIPS, 2019

replying_to: Replying to Concerns on robustness evaluations

content.title: the response to all reviewers
content.comment:
First of all, we want to thank R2, R3 & R4 for the active discussions of this paper. We do appreciate the reviewers’ efforts in helping us improve the quality of this paper! Nonetheless, it seems that we hold entirely different opinions on certain “concerns” and may not be able to reach an agreement during this rebuttal period. Given that, we decide to withdraw this paper. Before we try the next conference, we want to make the following clarifications:

***
(1) We already show the effectiveness of our method on the **very challenging ImageNet dataset**, and do not think missing results on small “warm-up” datasets like CIFAR-10 is a significant concern of this paper. 

Moreover, compared to ImageNet, studying robustness using small datasets like CIFAR-10 may not necessarily make the analysis easier or clearer, as multiple issues are mixed here. For example, [1] show that simply using early stopping (to prevent overfitting) can match all recent algorithmic improvements upon adversarial training in CIFAR-10. These results may suggest that the effectiveness of different methods is highly tailored to datasets, e.g., CIFAR-10 may weigh more on methods to alleviate overfitting than algorithmic improvements. Given our paper is mainly focusing on providing an algorithmic solution to improve robustness and adversarial training does not show overfitting in ImageNet, we believe choosing ImageNet to analyze our method will deliver a much more clear message than using small datasets like CIFAR-10.

***
(2) We also believe our experiments already provides an in-depth evaluation of our methods. 

We followed the suggestion from [2] to run sanity checks for our methods, e.g., if our models have gradient masking issues or if our attacker is properly set. Also by having private communications with the author in [2], we can confirm that our evaluations are properly done to rightfully access model robustness.

Moreover, compared to other advanced attacks, applying PGD attacker with enough attack iterations will provide on-par success attack rates on ImageNet, if models do not have any gradient masking issues. 

In light of the arguments above, we believe our current experiments are enough to support our claims, and will not include more evaluations against other attacks (as providing these additional results may not necessarily provide extra insights or contradict our current conclusions). 

Besides, we want to clarify that the purpose of releasing our code is mainly for facilitating the community to better study the problem of adversarial robustness learning in ImageNet, rather than asking the community to help us evaluate our models (as we already provide the basic in-depth analysis in the paper). But meanwhile, we do welcome all the researchers to invalid the arguments of this paper if any pitfalls are found in our evaluation framework.

***
(3) Similar to standard training on ImageNet, adversarial training here also produces a small variance. For example, by running ResNet-50 + SILU for 3 times, the difference between robustness is generally less than 0.5%. By considering that this difference is much smaller than the improvement that we got over the ReLU baseline (~9%), we therefore decide to not report variances in this paper.



***
[1] Rice, Leslie, Eric Wong, and J. Zico Kolter. "Overfitting in adversarially robust deep learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.11569 (2020).
[2] Carlini, Nicholas, et al. "On evaluating adversarial robustness." arXiv preprint arXiv:1902.06705 (2019).
